items.prompt: What does `git reflog` record?
choices: Every position a ref (like HEAD) has pointed to over time, on this local machine
A list of every file ever committed to the repository
The remote server's copy of the commit history
A list of merge conflicts that were ever resolved
items.explanation: Reflog is a local, per-ref log of ref movements — where HEAD or a branch has pointed, in order — not a file inventory or a remote-side record.
items.reference:
git reflog vs. git log
git log: history reachable from a ref right now
git reflog: every position a ref has pointed to, ever, on this machine

Why: reflog answers 'where has this ref been,' not 'what led up to this commit.'

items.prompt: How is `git reflog` different from `git log`?
choices: git log shows history reachable from a ref right now; git reflog shows every position that ref has ever occupied
They show exactly the same information, just formatted differently
git reflog only works on remote repositories, git log only works locally
git log shows file contents, git reflog shows commit messages only
items.explanation: git log walks the graph from a ref's current position. git reflog tracks the ref's own movement over time, independent of what's currently reachable.
items.reference:
git reflog vs. git log
git log: history reachable from a ref right now
git reflog: every position a ref has pointed to, ever, on this machine

Why: reflog answers 'where has this ref been,' not 'what led up to this commit.'

items.prompt: A teammate ran a command that made three commits disappear from `git log`. What's the most direct way to check whether git still remembers where HEAD was before that command?
choices: Run `git reflog` and look for HEAD's position just before the command that caused the disappearance
Re-clone the repository from the remote and hope the commits were pushed
Ask a coworker to email the commit diffs
There's no way to find this out once git log stops showing the commits
items.explanation: Reflog exists specifically for this: it records every move HEAD made, including the one right before the commits vanished from git log's view.
items.reference:
git reflog vs. git log
git log: history reachable from a ref right now
git reflog: every position a ref has pointed to, ever, on this machine

Why: reflog answers 'where has this ref been,' not 'what led up to this commit.'

items.prompt: After `git reset --hard <older-commit>`, does `git log` show the commits that were dropped?
choices: No — git log only shows what's reachable from HEAD's new position
Yes, git log always shows the full history regardless of resets
Only if `--all` is passed, and even then only for the last hour
Only the commit messages, not the commit contents
items.explanation: git log walks backward from HEAD's current position. Once reset moves HEAD, the dropped commits are simply outside that walk — even though the objects still exist.
items.reference:
After reset --hard
git log: only shows the new, shorter history
git reflog: still lists the dropped commits as HEAD@{1}, HEAD@{2}, ...

Why: reset moves the pointer; it does not erase the record of where the pointer used to be.

items.prompt: After the same `git reset --hard <older-commit>`, does `git reflog` still mention the dropped commits?
choices: Yes — as earlier HEAD@{n} entries, since reflog records HEAD's past positions, not just its current one
No, reflog is cleared by any reset command
Only if the commits were already pushed to a remote
Only if `git gc` has never been run on the repository
items.explanation: Reflog entries record moves, not current reachability — the dropped commits still show up as older HEAD@{n} entries right after the reset.
items.reference:
After reset --hard
git log: only shows the new, shorter history
git reflog: still lists the dropped commits as HEAD@{1}, HEAD@{2}, ...

Why: reset moves the pointer; it does not erase the record of where the pointer used to be.

items.prompt: What is a 'dangling commit,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A commit object that still exists on disk but has no branch or tag currently pointing to it
A commit that failed to apply due to a merge conflict
A commit made on a branch that was never pushed to any remote
A commit that modified more than one file
items.explanation: Dangling means unreachable from any current ref, not deleted — the object is still physically present in git's object store.
items.reference:
Dangling commit
Still exists in .git/objects
No branch or tag currently points to it
Recoverable until git gc prunes it

Why: a reset doesn't delete data, it just detaches a ref from it.

items.prompt: Does `git reset --hard` delete the commit objects it drops from history, immediately?
choices: No — it only moves the branch pointer; the objects remain on disk, now unreachable, until garbage collection
Yes, the objects are deleted from disk the instant the command finishes
Only the commit messages are deleted; the file contents remain
It depends on whether `--force` was also passed
items.explanation: reset --hard changes what the branch points to and updates the working tree — it does not touch the object store's contents directly.
items.reference:
Dangling commit
Still exists in .git/objects
No branch or tag currently points to it
Recoverable until git gc prunes it

Why: a reset doesn't delete data, it just detaches a ref from it.

items.prompt: What actually removes a dangling commit's data from a repository for good?
choices: Garbage collection (git gc, manual or automatic), once the object is both unreachable and past its retention window
The next `git commit` the user runs
Closing and reopening the terminal
Running `git status`
items.explanation: Only garbage collection actually prunes objects, and only after they're unreachable from any ref and old enough to be past the retention window.
items.reference:
Dangling commit
Still exists in .git/objects
No branch or tag currently points to it
Recoverable until git gc prunes it

Why: a reset doesn't delete data, it just detaches a ref from it.

items.prompt: What is `ORIG_HEAD`?
choices: A special ref git sets automatically right before an operation like reset, merge, or rebase moves HEAD significantly
The very first commit ever made in the repository
A backup branch that git creates automatically every night
The commit that a pull request originally branched from
items.explanation: ORIG_HEAD is git's automatic one-step-back pointer, updated right before history-rewriting operations — a quick undo target, separate from the full reflog.
items.reference:
ORIG_HEAD
Set automatically before a big HEAD-moving operation
One-step undo pointer, distinct from the full reflog

Why: reflog has the full history of moves; ORIG_HEAD is just 'one step back.'

items.prompt: How does `ORIG_HEAD` differ from `git reflog`?
choices: ORIG_HEAD is a single one-step-back pointer; reflog is a full ordered history of every position a ref has occupied
They are two different names for exactly the same feature
ORIG_HEAD only exists on remote repositories, reflog only exists locally
ORIG_HEAD tracks file changes, reflog tracks only branch names
items.explanation: ORIG_HEAD gives you one step of undo automatically; reflog gives you the entire sequence of moves, which is why reflog can recover from further back than one step.
items.reference:
ORIG_HEAD
Set automatically before a big HEAD-moving operation
One-step undo pointer, distinct from the full reflog

Why: reflog has the full history of moves; ORIG_HEAD is just 'one step back.'

items.prompt: What problem does `git bisect` solve?
choices: Finding which commit, among many, first introduced a bug
Recovering commits dropped by a reset --hard
Merging two branches automatically without conflicts
Compressing the repository's object store
items.explanation: Bisect is a regression-hunting tool: given a known-good and a known-bad commit, it narrows down which commit in between first broke things.
items.reference:
git bisect
Different problem from reflog: 'which commit broke this?'
Binary search over a good..bad range of commits

Why: reflog recovers lost positions; bisect finds a bad commit among many good ones.

items.prompt: Could `git reflog` be used to find which of 500 already-merged commits introduced a regression?
choices: No — reflog only records ref movements on your machine, not which historical commit is responsible for a bug
Yes, reflog is specifically designed to test each commit for a regression
Yes, but only for regressions found within the last hour
Yes, as long as the regression is described in a commit message
items.explanation: Reflog and bisect solve unrelated problems. Reflog can't tell you which commit is buggy — that's what bisect's good/bad testing is for.
items.reference:
git bisect
Different problem from reflog: 'which commit broke this?'
Binary search over a good..bad range of commits

Why: reflog recovers lost positions; bisect finds a bad commit among many good ones.

items.prompt: What does 'bisect' mean in the context of `git bisect`?
choices: Repeatedly splitting the range of candidate commits in half, testing the midpoint, and discarding the half that can't contain the culprit
Splitting a single commit into two smaller commits
Comparing two branches side by side in a diff view
Running every commit's tests simultaneously in parallel
items.explanation: Bisect is literally a binary search over commit history — each test halves the remaining range of suspects.
items.reference:
git bisect
Different problem from reflog: 'which commit broke this?'
Binary search over a good..bad range of commits

Why: reflog recovers lost positions; bisect finds a bad commit among many good ones.

items.prompt: In a reflog line like `e7c9d14 HEAD@{1}: commit: add rate limiter tests`, what does the `1` in `HEAD@{1}` mean?
choices: HEAD was at this commit one move before its current position
This is the first commit ever made in the repository
There is exactly 1 file changed in this commit
This commit is 1 day old
items.explanation: HEAD@{n} is a relative index counting backward through HEAD's move history — {0} is now, {1} is one move earlier, and so on.
items.reference:
A reflog entry
sha HEAD@{n}: reason: detail
n=0 is always the current position, n=1 is one move before that

Why: each entry pairs a commit id, a relative index, and a human-readable reason for the move.

items.prompt: Which reflog index always refers to HEAD's current position, right now?
choices: HEAD@{0}
HEAD@{1}
Whichever index has the highest number
There is no fixed index for 'current' — it changes randomly
items.explanation: HEAD@{0} is always 'where HEAD is right this second' — every other index counts backward in moves from there.
items.reference:
A reflog entry
sha HEAD@{n}: reason: detail
n=0 is always the current position, n=1 is one move before that

Why: each entry pairs a commit id, a relative index, and a human-readable reason for the move.

items.prompt: A reflog entry shows `reset: moving to origin/main` next to a commit id. What part of the entry does 'reset: moving to origin/main' represent?
choices: The reason git recorded for that particular ref movement
The exact time the move happened
The name of the person who ran the command
The number of files changed by that operation
items.explanation: Every reflog entry pairs a commit id and index with a reason string describing what kind of operation caused HEAD to move there.
items.reference:
A reflog entry
sha HEAD@{n}: reason: detail
n=0 is always the current position, n=1 is one move before that

Why: each entry pairs a commit id, a relative index, and a human-readable reason for the move.

items.prompt: By default, how long does a reflog entry for a commit that's the *only* thing referencing an otherwise-unreachable commit stick around before it's eligible for pruning?
choices: 30 days (gc.reflogExpireUnreachable)
90 days (gc.reflogExpire)
1 hour
Forever, unless manually deleted
items.explanation: gc.reflogExpireUnreachable defaults to 30 days — the shorter window, since these entries are the sole thing keeping the commit's data alive.
items.reference:
Default expiry windows
gc.reflogExpire: 90 days (still reachable some other way)
gc.reflogExpireUnreachable: 30 days (no other ref points to it)

Why: two clocks have to both run out before git gc actually prunes an object.

items.prompt: Is a commit dropped by `reset --hard` two days ago at real risk of being pruned by the next `git gc` run, under default settings?
choices: No — two days is far inside both the 30-day and 90-day default expiry windows
Yes, git gc prunes anything not on the current branch within an hour
Yes, because reset --hard bypasses the expiry windows entirely
It depends only on the size of the commit, not its age
items.explanation: Both default windows are measured in weeks, not hours — a two-day-old drop is nowhere close to either expiry threshold.
items.reference:
Default expiry windows
gc.reflogExpire: 90 days (still reachable some other way)
gc.reflogExpireUnreachable: 30 days (no other ref points to it)

Why: two clocks have to both run out before git gc actually prunes an object.

items.prompt: Roughly how many tests does bisect need to find the culprit among 500 commits?
choices: About 9 (roughly log2(500))
About 250 (half of 500)
Exactly 500, one per commit
Exactly 2, regardless of how many commits there are
items.explanation: Bisect converges in roughly log2(n) tests because each test halves the remaining range — log2(500) is about 8.97, so about 9 tests.
items.reference:
Bisect convergence
Each test halves the remaining range of commits
Roughly log2(n) tests for n commits

Why: 500 commits converges in about 9 tests, not 500 one-by-one checks.

items.prompt: Why does bisect need far fewer tests than the total number of commits in the range?
choices: Because each test result discards half of the remaining candidates, not just one
Because bisect randomly skips most commits without testing them at all
Because git already knows which commit is bad before bisect starts
Because bisect only tests commits with certain commit message keywords
items.explanation: The efficiency comes from halving, not skipping — every single test still rules out real candidates, just half the remaining range at a time instead of one commit at a time.
items.reference:
Bisect convergence
Each test halves the remaining range of commits
Roughly log2(n) tests for n commits

Why: 500 commits converges in about 9 tests, not 500 one-by-one checks.

items.prompt: If the number of commits between the last known-good point and the bug report doubles, roughly how much does the number of bisect tests needed change?
choices: It increases by about 1 test, not by doubling
It also doubles
It stays exactly the same no matter what
It quadruples
items.explanation: log2(2n) = log2(n) + 1 — doubling the range only costs one additional test, which is the whole point of a logarithmic search.
items.reference:
Bisect convergence
Each test halves the remaining range of commits
Roughly log2(n) tests for n commits

Why: 500 commits converges in about 9 tests, not 500 one-by-one checks.

items.prompt: Bisect tests the midpoint commit and it turns out bad. What does bisect conclude about the culprit's location?
choices: The culprit is at the midpoint or somewhere earlier in the range
The culprit is definitely exactly at the midpoint
The culprit must be somewhere after the midpoint
The test result tells bisect nothing new
items.explanation: A 'bad' result at the midpoint only narrows the range to the midpoint-or-earlier half; it doesn't pinpoint the culprit until the range shrinks to one commit.
items.reference:
good / bad markers
good: this commit doesn't have the bug
bad: this commit has the bug

Why: bisect narrows the range using your test result at the midpoint, not the midpoint's content.

items.prompt: Bisect tests the midpoint commit and it turns out good. Which half of the remaining range does bisect discard?
choices: Everything from the start of the range up through the midpoint
Everything from the midpoint through the end of the range
Bisect discards nothing and re-tests the same commit
Bisect discards the entire range and starts over
items.explanation: A 'good' midpoint means the culprit must be strictly after it — everything up to and including the midpoint is now ruled out.
items.reference:
good / bad markers
good: this commit doesn't have the bug
bad: this commit has the bug

Why: bisect narrows the range using your test result at the midpoint, not the midpoint's content.

items.prompt: If a coworker runs a destructive `reset --hard` on their own laptop, can you use *your* reflog to recover their lost commits?
choices: No — reflog is local to each machine's own .git directory, it doesn't cover anyone else's history
Yes, reflog is synced automatically to a shared server
Yes, as long as you both work on the same branch name
Yes, but only if you're both connected to the same Wi-Fi network
items.explanation: Reflog lives entirely inside one local .git directory — it has no mechanism for syncing across machines, so it can only ever help recover history on the machine where the mistake happened.
items.reference:
Reflog's scope
Local only — lives in .git on your machine
Never pushed, never shared, never cloned

Why: reflog can't recover a coworker's mistake on their own machine, or survive a fresh clone.

items.prompt: Does a fresh `git clone` of a repository include the original machine's reflog?
choices: No — a clone starts with a fresh, empty reflog on the new machine
Yes, clone always copies the full reflog history along with the commits
Only if `--mirror` is passed to git clone
Only for the default branch, not other branches
items.explanation: Reflog is never transferred by clone, fetch, or push — each local repository builds its own reflog purely from operations run on that machine.
items.reference:
Reflog's scope
Local only — lives in .git on your machine
Never pushed, never shared, never cloned

Why: reflog can't recover a coworker's mistake on their own machine, or survive a fresh clone.

items.prompt: A `git push --force` overwrote a branch on the shared remote. Can the pusher's local reflog help recover the overwritten commits on the remote itself?
choices: It can help the pusher recover their own local copy, but it does nothing for the remote's state directly
Yes, reflog automatically restores the remote branch to its previous state
No, reflog is completely useless in this situation for anyone
Yes, but only within 5 minutes of the force-push
items.explanation: The pusher's local reflog still remembers the old position and lets them recover locally, but reflog has no reach onto the remote server — restoring the remote branch requires someone to push the recovered commits back up.
items.reference:
Reflog's scope
Local only — lives in .git on your machine
Never pushed, never shared, never cloned

Why: reflog can't recover a coworker's mistake on their own machine, or survive a fresh clone.

items.prompt: Implement `bisectSearch(commits, isBad)`, matching this unit's L3: binary-search an ordered array of commits (good ones first, then bad ones, with exactly one good→bad flip point) for the first bad commit, returning `{ culprit, steps }`.

tests.description: finds the culprit in a simple flip
handles a single-commit range

items.explanation: The loop keeps a [lo, hi] range of candidate indices and halves it on every test: a bad midpoint means the culprit is at or before it (hi = mid), a good midpoint means it's strictly after (lo = mid + 1). items.prompt: After finding the dropped commit's position at `HEAD@{1}` in the reflog, what is the safer first recovery step, per this unit's L3 transcript?
choices: Create a named branch pointing at HEAD@{1} (e.g. `git branch recovery HEAD@{1}`) before doing anything else
Immediately run `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` with no other steps
Delete the current branch and start a brand new repository
Force-push the current (already-reset) branch to overwrite the remote
items.explanation: Anchoring the old tip to a stable branch name first removes the risk of HEAD@{1} referring to something else after a subsequent command — a named branch doesn't move on its own.
items.reference:
Recovering the dropped tip
git reflog -> find HEAD@{n} for the old tip
git branch recovery HEAD@{n} -> anchor it to a name first
git reset --hard recovery -> restore it

Why: anchoring to a branch name first avoids relying on a moving HEAD@{n} index.

items.explanation: HEAD@{n} indices are relative to HEAD's current position, so they shift after every further command — a real risk if you run more than one step during a recovery, which is why anchoring to a branch name first is safer.
items.reference:
Recovering the dropped tip
git reflog -> find HEAD@{n} for the old tip
git branch recovery HEAD@{n} -> anchor it to a name first
git reset --hard recovery -> restore it

Why: anchoring to a branch name first avoids relying on a moving HEAD@{n} index.
